title: Apple's Next Ultra-Slim iPhone Air 2 Tipped for 2027 Launch With Bigger Battery, 48MP Ultra-Wide Camera and A20 Pro Chip
summary: Apple's Next Ultra-Slim iPhone Air 2 Tipped for 2027 Launch With Bigger Battery, 48MP Ultra-Wide…
detailed: Apple's second-generation ultra-slim handset is taking shape in the rumor mill, with a prominent Chinese leaker pointing to a trio of headline upgrades for the iPhone Air 2: a next-generation A-series processor, a larger battery and a second 48-megapixel rear camera.
The iPhone Air 2 is tipped to gain a 48-megapixel ultra-wide-angle sensor alongside the existing 48-megapixel main camera, giving the ultra-thin line a dual-lens rear setup for the first time.

The timeline itself has shifted repeatedly in the rumor cycle: the first Air was widely expected to be branded the iPhone 17 Air before Apple settled on the simpler name, and the successor has been variously placed in spring 2027 and early 2027, when it is expected to share a launch window with the lower-cost iPhone 18.

The current Air starts at $1,099 in the United States, after Apple raised prices across its older models when it introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo in September 2026, and at ¥189,800 in Japan.
sentences: Apple's second-generation ultra-slim handset is taking shape in the rumor mill, with a prominent Chinese leaker pointing to a trio of headline upgrades for the iPhone Air 2: a next-generation A-series processor, a larger battery and a second 48-megapixel rear camera.
The device is expected to arrive in early 2027, according to Digital Chat Station, the account that has tracked Apple's supply chain plans for years.

The leaker's account, summarized in coverage by Notebookcheck, describes a phone that keeps the current model's 6.55-inch OLED panel and its LTPO backplane, which supports a variable refresh rate up to 120 Hz at a 1.5K resolution.
The chassis, meanwhile, is said to slim down to 5.2 millimeters, a 0.4-millimeter reduction from the first-generation Air, even as Apple adds hardware inside it.
That added hardware centers on imaging.
The iPhone Air 2 is tipped to gain a 48-megapixel ultra-wide-angle sensor alongside the existing 48-megapixel main camera, giving the ultra-thin line a dual-lens rear setup for the first time.
On the silicon side, the phone is expected to move to the A20 family, most likely the A20 Pro, the 2-nanometer chip that already powers the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo.

Geeky-Gadgets, citing earlier supply-chain reporting, expects roughly 15% better performance and up to 30% greater energy efficiency from the A20 generation, along with a smaller TrueDepth array that could shrink the Dynamic Island.
Battery capacity is the other frequently cited fix.
The same report puts the cell at about 3,500 mAh, up from 3,149 mAh, a modest gain that would be amplified by the new chip's efficiency.

It also points to a redesigned thermal system intended to prevent the throttling that can afflict slim handsets during sustained gaming or video work, and to Apple's in-house C2 modem, which would succeed the C1X modem Apple designed for the current Air and could add satellite connectivity for emergency messaging outside cellular coverage.
Apple has not confirmed any of these details, and the company does not comment on unannounced products.

The timeline itself has shifted repeatedly in the rumor cycle: the first Air was widely expected to be branded the iPhone 17 Air before Apple settled on the simpler name, and the successor has been variously placed in spring 2027 and early 2027, when it is expected to share a launch window with the lower-cost iPhone 18.
Pricing remains the least certain element.
The same outlet floated a range of $999 to $1,999 depending on configuration, a spread wide enough to be treated with caution.

The current Air starts at $1,099 in the United States, after Apple raised prices across its older models when it introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo in September 2026, and at ¥189,800 in Japan.

A spring 2027 release would put the device roughly 18 months after the original, a cadence that would depart from Apple's annual iPhone refresh and suggests the Air line may settle into a less frequent cycle.
Note: Current-model figures are based on published specifications and prior reporting; iPhone Air 2 figures are unconfirmed leaks.
The stakes for Apple are commercial as much as technical.

The ultra-thin category is a design statement meant to anchor the top of the lineup, but thin bodies leave little room for battery cells and cooling hardware, and early reviews of the first Air focused heavily on endurance.

A larger cell paired with a 2-nanometer chip would let Apple argue that the trade-off between slimness and stamina has narrowed, while a second rear lens removes a conspicuous gap against the Pro models.
For suppliers, the reported specifications imply a meaningful shift in component demand.
The C1X already replaced Qualcomm silicon in the current Air, making a C2 the second generation of Apple's in-house modem rather than a first break from Qualcomm.
A dual 48-megapixel camera module, meanwhile, raises sensor and lens orders.

The 2-nanometer node also points to continued heavy reliance on TSMC's most advanced manufacturing capacity: Apple took nearly half of the foundry's initial N2 output when mass production began in August 2025.
Investors have grown sensitive to iPhone unit growth as the smartphone market matures, and the Air line is watched as a test of whether Apple can charge a premium for form factor alone.

A spring 2027 launch would place the device in a quieter part of the calendar, potentially smoothing seasonal revenue but also separating it from the flagship September cycle that drives the bulk of upgrade activity.
Leaker accounts have a mixed record, and specifications can change late in development, particularly around battery chemistry and camera module thickness in a chassis this thin.
The pricing figures circulating so far span a range too broad to be actionable, and Apple has a history of trimming features from slim devices when engineering constraints bite.
Separately, Apple is managing a quality issue on a different product.

The company acknowledged a display defect affecting a small number of its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and said it would replace affected units free of charge regardless of whether they were bought outright or through a carrier, according to Apple's statement reported by Naver Finance.
The company said the problem was confined to a limited early production batch and did not elaborate on the cause, and that it had set aside replacement inventory separate from new-sale stock.
The iPhone Duo went on sale on October 23 at $1,999 in the United States and ¥364,800 in Japan; replacing its inner display out of warranty costs $999, roughly half the entry price.
